title: Normalization and Many-to-Many Relationships
summary: Learn why repeating data in a single table causes update anomalies, how splitting tables into separate entities removes that redundancy, and how a junction table resolves a many-to-many relationship into two ordinary one-to-many links.

steps.title: One big table — and its hidden cost
steps.lede: Imagine every order row repeating the customer's name and city. That design looks simple, but it carries a real cost.

blocks.text: Imagine, instead of separate customers and orders tables, one wide orders table that repeats each customer's name and city on every order row they place. A customer with five orders would have their name and city written out five separate times. Normalization is the process of determining how much redundancy exists in a table, with the goal of transforming the schema to remove that redundancy.

left.title: orders_flat (un-normalized)
left.alt_text: A single flat orders table with columns order_id, customer_name, customer_city, delivery_minutes. customer_name and customer_city are marked as repeating on every order row — the un-normalized design that causes update anomalies.

right.caption: customers table — name and city stored once; orders link back via customer_id

blocks.takeaway: Moving customer_name and customer_city into their own table stores each value exactly once. The orders table keeps only customer_id to link back — no more repeated values, no update anomaly.

steps.title: Update anomalies and the fix
steps.lede: Repeated data doesn't just waste space — it creates a consistency trap every time a value needs to change.

blocks.text: Redundant data is generally undesirable because it causes problems maintaining consistency after updates. If a customer's city changes, every one of the repeated rows must be updated. Missing even one leaves inconsistent data — an update anomaly, where the same customer appears to live in two different cities depending on which order row you read.

One way to remove the redundancy is to move the data that would otherwise repeat across many rows into a new, separate table, linked back to the original record by a key column — exactly the split into customers (name and city stored once each) and orders (which keeps only customer_id to identify the customer) that the QuickShip schema already uses.

steps.title: Splitting a table to remove redundancy
steps.lede: A single orders table stores customer_id, customer_name, customer_city, and delivery_minutes on every row. Which change removes the redundancy?

public.prompt: A single orders table stores customer_id, customer_name, customer_city, and delivery_minutes on every row. A customer with five orders has their name and city repeated five times. Which change removes that redundancy?

options.text: Move customer_name and customer_city into a separate customers table, linked back by customer_id
Add an index on customer_name to speed up lookups
Replace repeated customer_name values with NULL after the first row
Sort the table by customer_id so repeated rows are grouped together

opt_split.message: Correct. Moving the repeating data into a separate table and linking it by key is exactly how normalization removes redundancy — each customer's name and city is stored once.

opt_index.message: Not quite. An index speeds up queries but does not remove the repeated data; the name and city are still stored five times.

opt_null.message: Not quite. Replacing repeated values with NULL would break the data — you would lose the customer's name and city for most orders. Normalization moves the data to a separate table, not removes it.

opt_sort.message: Not quite. Sorting groups the repeated rows visually but does not remove the redundancy — the name and city are still stored five times, and an update anomaly is still possible.

correct.message: Exactly right. Splitting the repeating data into a separate table and linking by key is the normalization move that removes redundancy.

incorrect.message: Remember: normalization removes redundancy by moving repeating data into a new table linked by a key column.

hints: Think about what 'removing redundancy' means — the data should be stored only once.
Which option actually changes where the data lives, rather than just changing how it looks or how fast it can be found?

steps.title: Find the redundancy and redesign the table
steps.lede: The QuickShip orders table has customer details repeated on every row. Identify the redundant columns and redesign the schema into two tables that remove the update anomaly.

public.instructions: The table below shows a customers table where a data entry error has introduced a duplicate row. Flag the cell that reveals the redundancy problem — the repeated customer_id that would cause an update anomaly if the customer's details changed.

issues.explanation: customer_id 1 appears twice. This duplicate row means that if Amara Okafor's city changes, both rows must be updated — missing one creates an update anomaly where the same customer appears to live in two different cities.

decoys.message: customer_id 2 (Emeka Nwosu) appears only once — no redundancy here.
customer_id 3 (Fatima Bello) appears only once — no redundancy here.

grading.wrong_category_message: You found the duplicate row, but check the category. A repeated customer_id is a redundancy problem — it creates an update anomaly risk, not a clean record.
grading.completion_message: Well done. You identified the duplicate row for customer_id 1. Storing the same customer twice means any update to their details must be applied to both rows — missing one leaves inconsistent data.

correct.message: Correct. The duplicate row for customer_id 1 is the redundancy problem. If the customer's city changes, both rows must be updated — missing one creates an update anomaly.

incorrect.message: Look for a customer_id that appears more than once. That repeated row is the redundancy that normalization removes.

hints: Scan the customer_id column for any value that appears more than once.
A redundant row means the same customer's details are stored twice — what happens if their city changes?

steps.title: When both sides can have many — the junction table
steps.lede: One order can include several products, and one product can appear in several orders. That shape of relationship needs a different solution.

blocks.text: One order can include several products, and one product — say, a rice bag — can show up in several different orders. Neither side is limited to 'one' the way customer/order was. A many-to-many (M:N) relationship cannot be implemented directly in the relational model; it is resolved into two one-to-many relationships using a composite entity, also called a junction or bridge table.

Between orders and products, that junction table — order_items — holds one row for every order/product pairing: order 101 paired with the rice bag, order 101 paired with cooking oil, order 103 paired with the rice bag again. Each pairing is its own row; the two sides connect through two one-to-many links.

blocks.title: Many-to-many resolved via order_items junction table
blocks.alt_text: ERD showing orders linked to order_items (1:N) and products linked to order_items (1:N). order_items has a composite primary key of order_id and product_id, both foreign keys. The many-to-many between orders and products is resolved through the junction table.

steps.title: What goes inside the junction table
steps.lede: The junction table must carry the right columns — and those columns together form its primary key.

blocks.text: The junction table must contain at least the primary keys of the two original tables, used as foreign keys, and may also contain additional attributes of its own. order_items holds order_id (a foreign key to orders) and product_id (a foreign key to products). The combination of those two foreign keys makes the primary key of the junction table — the pair (order_id, product_id) together is unique, since the same order won't list the same product twice.

steps.title: Resolving many-to-many with a junction table
steps.lede: Watch two failed designs — storing many students in a class row, or many classes in a student row — then see how a junction table fixes both.

blocks.group_title: Resolving many-to-many with a junction table

segments.label: Why a many-to-many needs a junction table: two failed designs, then two one-to-many links
segments.summary: A chalkboard walk-through of students and classes. A design with several student columns in the class record, and another with many class columns in the student record, both waste space and break down, showing the relationship cannot be stored directly. The fix is an intermediary table, also called a junction table, which turns it into two one-to-many relationships, and the new table's columns are foreign keys pointing back to the class and the student.

bridge.before: A long chalkboard clip. Watch the two failed designs first, since they motivate the junction table, then the redraw into two one-to-many links.
bridge.after: Within this range the clip does not say the pair of keys forms the junction table's primary key, or that it can hold extra attributes. The text above covers both.

steps.title: Designing the junction table's keys
steps.lede: A junction table called enrollments resolves a many-to-many between students and courses. Which columns must it contain, and what forms its primary key?

public.prompt: A junction table called enrollments resolves a many-to-many relationship between students and courses. Which columns must it contain, and what forms its primary key?

options.text: It must contain student_id and course_id as foreign keys; the pair (student_id, course_id) forms the primary key
It must contain only student_id as a foreign key; course_id is optional
It must contain student_id and course_id, but needs a separate enrollment_id as its primary key
It must contain student_name and course_name so the data is self-contained

opt_correct.message: Correct. The junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys, and the combination of those two foreign keys forms the primary key of the junction table.

opt_one_fk.message: Not quite. A junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys — both student_id and course_id are required to record which student is enrolled in which course.

opt_new_pk.message: Not quite. While a separate surrogate key is sometimes added, the combination of the two foreign keys (student_id, course_id) is what makes the primary key of the junction table — that pair is unique because the same student won't enrol in the same course twice.

opt_no_fk.message: Not quite. Storing names instead of keys reintroduces redundancy and breaks the relational link. The junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys.

correct.message: Exactly right. The junction table holds the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys, and their combination is the primary key.

incorrect.message: Remember: the junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys, and those two keys together form the junction table's primary key.

hints: What two pieces of information does the junction table need to record a single enrollment?
The primary key of the junction table must uniquely identify each pairing — what combination of columns achieves that?

steps.title: Design a junction table for students and courses
steps.lede: A students table and a courses table have a many-to-many relationship. Select the columns the junction table needs and identify the composite primary key.

public.intro: The order_items table is the junction table that resolves the many-to-many relationship between orders and products. Each row records one order/product pairing.

tasks.prompt: Select the column that is a foreign key referencing the orders table.
Select the column that is a foreign key referencing the products table.
Select a cell in the order_id column that is part of the composite primary key for the first pairing (order 101 with the rice bag, product 10).
Select a cell in the product_id column that completes the composite primary key for that same first pairing.

task_fk_order.correct: Correct. order_id is a foreign key referencing orders.order_id — it links each row back to the order it belongs to.
task_fk_order.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the column that references the orders table by storing the order's primary key.

task_fk_product.correct: Correct. product_id is a foreign key referencing products.product_id — it links each row to the product included in that order.
task_fk_product.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the column that references the products table by storing the product's primary key.

task_pk_pair_order.correct: Correct. order_id 101 is the first half of the composite primary key for this pairing.
task_pk_pair_order.incorrect: Not quite. Select the order_id value in the row where order 101 is paired with product 10 (the rice bag).

task_pk_pair_product.correct: Correct. product_id 10 completes the composite primary key (101, 10) — this pair is unique because the same order won't list the same product twice.
task_pk_pair_product.incorrect: Not quite. Select the product_id value in the row where order 101 is paired with product 10 (the rice bag).

correct.message: Well done. You identified both foreign key columns and the composite primary key pair — the two foreign keys together uniquely identify each order/product pairing.

incorrect.message: Review the junction table structure. Each column is a foreign key to one of the original tables, and together they form the composite primary key.

hints: Each column in the junction table is a foreign key to one of the two original tables — which table does each column reference?
The composite primary key is the pair of foreign keys — find the row where order 101 is paired with product 10.

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Two ideas that shape every well-designed relational schema.

blocks.text: Normalization removes redundancy by moving repeated data into its own table, linked back by a key — the customers/orders split is normalization already applied. When both sides of a relationship can have many, a junction table resolves it into two one-to-many links; order_items holds a foreign key to each side, and the pair of those keys forms the junction table's primary key.

remediation_steps.title: Splitting a table: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Compare a merged table with repeated values against the split design.

blocks.text: Un-normalized: one orders table with columns order_id, customer_name, customer_city, delivery_minutes. Customer Amara Okafor in Lagos appears on rows 101 and 103 — her city is stored twice. If she moves, both rows must be updated; missing one creates an update anomaly. Normalized: a customers table stores name and city once (customer_id 1 → Amara Okafor, Lagos). The orders table keeps only customer_id 1 on both rows — one update to customers fixes everything.

remediation_steps.title: Junction table keys: a clear contrast
remediation_steps.lede: Two designs — one missing a foreign key, one correct.

blocks.text: Incomplete: order_items has only order_id — it can't identify which product is in the order, so the link to products is broken. Correct: order_items has order_id (foreign key to orders) and product_id (foreign key to products). The pair (order_id, product_id) is the composite primary key — unique because the same order won't list the same product twice. Both foreign keys are required; either one alone is insufficient.
